title: Grid Reference to Postcode Finder: NGR Lookup
description: Find postcodes near the approximate centre of a British grid square using postcodes.io.
summary_sentence: The postcode search uses an approximate square centre; results depend on service coverage and the uncorrected datum difference.
quick_answer: The tool takes the centre of a British National Grid square, converts it approximately to latitude and longitude without a datum shift, then asks postcodes.io for nearby postcodes. These are not necessarily addresses within the square.

Field reports recorded by grid reference get their postal line filled in for correspondence and invoicing.
A rural venue known by its map reference acquires the postcode guests' phones can navigate to.
Historic site files cite references; attaching the modern postcode makes the archive searchable by everyone else's tools.
A point in open fields has no postcode of its own — the finder returns the NEAREST postcode the data holds and labels it as such. Nearest is orientation, not a postal address for the field.
The conversion does not apply a WGS84–OSGB36 datum shift. That approximation can change which postcodes appear near the search point.

faq: Whose postcode data does it use?
postcodes.io — the open service built on the Office for National Statistics and Royal Mail-derived open data. Its record is the finder's record.
A postcode for a mountain summit?
The nearest valley postcode is what exists to return — labelled nearest. Summits do not receive post, and the finder does not pretend otherwise.
Old postcodes vanish from current data; a historic address's code may return its successor area instead.
The provider returns nearby postcodes within its search coverage. The query point is an approximate square centre without a datum shift, so verify the result.
Can I use the postcode for navigation?
A nearby postcode is not necessarily an address in the grid square. Verify it with authoritative address data before navigation or delivery.
Large organisations hold dedicated postcodes; a point inside one can return that code — correct, if occasionally surprising.
